column43: ""In the H-2Db/gp33 complex [PDB: 1S7U], both residues p4Y and p6F project out of the peptide binding cleft, acting as potential main TCR contacts. The escape mutants pY4F[PDB: 1S7X] and pF6L [PDB: 1S7V] could thus be explained by impaired TCR recognition rather than by impaired MHC binding. However, the structural impacts of these two conservative substitutions are different. The pY4F mutation does not result in any modifications other than the removal of the tyrosine hydroxyl group, whereas the conserved pF6L substitution results in changes in the potential TCR contact residues that probably affect the sensitive regions of the TCR through direct sterical clashes and/or the introduction of cavities at the TCR/pMHC interface. The pF6L mutation results in shifts in the central portion variant peptide (residues p4 to p7). The introduction of a less bulky leucine side chain causes a subtle movement of this portion of the peptide toward the alpha1 domain. The largest movements take place in residues p4Y and p6L. The movements of residues p4 and p6 would most likely result in the creation of cavities at the pMHC/p14TCR interface and/or clashes with the CDR3alpha or CDR3beta of the TCR. Finally, the shift introduced in the main chain of residue p6 induces small movements in residues S150, A152, and H155 of the alpha2 domain toward the mutated peptide. Most of these residues have been identified as TCR contacts."" Contacts here are provided as in the paper describing the structure [PDB: 1N5A] [PMID: 12479822] with no modifications as described in the curated paper.

The side chains of P1-Glu, P4-Phe, and P9-Glu are bound in deep pockets, forming major anchor residues, whereas side chains of P6-Pro and P7-Ser lie in shallow pockets, forming minor anchor residues. P5 and P8 residues exhibit high solvent accessibility, with their side chains projecting out of the cleft, and hence are available for TCR ligation. The flanking residues P-2-Ser, P-1-Gly, P10-Asn, and P11-Pro might also play a role in TCR recognition. Eight of twelve hydrogen bonds formed between the peptide backbone and HLA DQ8 are conserved in most MHC class II structures and are mediated via Arg53alpha, Asn62beta, Asn69beta, Trp61beta, Asn82beta, and His81beta. If glutamate (Glu) were substituted for glutamine (Gln) at either of the P1 or P9 positions (to resemble the core of the nondeamidated native form of the alpha-gliadin DQ8 immunodominant determinant), the complex bonding network within these respective pockets would be disrupted, thereby leading to a less stable complex.

Specifically the SAG only contacts epitope residues P-1 and P2 and forms a single hydrogen bond between SAG residue D: E211 and the amino group epitope residue P-1: K307. Only some small side chain rearrangements were observed. One of them is the side chain of MHC residue B: Q70 which, in the MHC-epitope complex, forms one hydrogen bond to epitope residue P4: Q311; but in the SAG-MHC/epitope complex it shifts and forms two hydrogen bonds to the same epitope residue.

They are bound to K-2-Hb with almost the same conformation, especially in the central part between residues 3-p. The two epitopes main chains have very similar conformations in the N-terminal part (residues 1-6), but the C-terminus (residues 7-9) of rDBM shifts towards the peptide binding groove by 0.8Å. This is because the anchor residue C: I9; moves deeper into MHC pocket F. The side chains of residues 1,4,6 in both epitopes have very similar conformations. In epitope gp33(V3L), there are shifts in the main chains of residues 2-6. The epitope moves towards the MHC alpha1 domain in the peptide binding groove. Participating residues in this movement are A2, L3 and Y4. The peptide binding grooves of the two MHC residues (K-2-Hb/rDBM K-2-Hb/gp33) have similar conformations at the epitope N-terminal part, but the groove is wider at the C-terminus in the K-2-Hb/rDBM complex. Epitope residue side chains I: W4, H8; extend out of the binding groove and are predicted to interact with the TCR (especially W4). By using the two determined structures and molecular modeling, mutations were introduced at epitope position 4 to study their effect on TCR binding. An R4 substitution would not fit in the space available, and the R side chain would extend out of the binding groove and interfere with TCR binding. L4 and E4 mutations do not cause structural clashes, as with the S4 mutation in the variant epitope structure. column43: The SSLENARAYV peptide adopts an extended conformation and forms anchoring interactions with the alpha1-alpha2 domains at the peptide positions P2-Ser, P5-Asn, and P10-Val. Additionally there are vdw contacts between the MHC molecule and the side chain of P1-Ser, and the backbone at P4-Glu, P6-Ala, and P9-Tyr. The region of the peptide between P6-Ala and P9-Tyr extends prominently from the peptide-binding groove and is significantly solvent exposed. This includes the site of the P6-Phe to P6-Ala mutation and the neighboring P7-Arg. Comparing the F6A structure and the wild-type H2-DbPA [PDB: 1WBY], there is little movement between the alpha1 and alpha2 domains of the MHC molecule. The two peptides adopt equivalent conformations, overlaying with an rmsd of 0.16 Å at the Calpha position, with identical anchoring interactions to the MHC molecules. The major difference between the two structures occurs at the solvent-exposed C-terminal region of the F6A mutant peptide. column43: The VLH peptide adopts an extended structure in the antigen binding groove, with retention of stabilizing interactions from MHC residues to the peptide N and C terminus. The canonical Leu-2 anchor residue is oriented in a standard position in the B pocket, forming extensive contacts with surrounding hydrophobic residues. In contrast, the C-terminal anchor residue is alanine, which is poorly represented at this position in HLA-A2 peptides (21) and forms only extremely scant contacts with the F pocket. The paucity of contacts with Ala-9 suggested that interactions mediated by secondary anchor residues, such as the polymorphic His-3, might substantially affect the overall stability of the pMHC complex. The His-3 side chain fits relatively snugly in the D pocket, forming van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions with Tyr-99, Tyr-159, and Leu-156 lining the pocket. In addition, His-3 mediates indirect contacts to Gln-155 and the peptide main chain at P5 via a single bridging water molecule. These contacts, and the fact that they are mediated by the imidazole ring, suggested that the His-3 side chain substantially stabilized the pMHC interaction relative to VLR peptide (His3->Arg mutant).

column43: The two major pockets, A′ and F′, are located deep inside the CD1 protein and each accommodate one alkyl chain of the sulfatide ligand. The sulfated galactose headgroup is then positioned above the binding groove at the interface between both pockets. As the A′ pocket is larger in volume than the F′ pocket, the synthetic sulfatide binds such that the longer cis-tetracosenoyl fatty acid (C24:1) occupies the A′ pocket, whereas the shorter sphingosine backbone (C18) is inserted into the F′ pocket. As the sulfatide alkyl chains then fully occupy both binding pockets, the previously reported spacer lipid [PDB: 1Z5L] is not observed in the CD1d binding groove. Seven hydrogen bonds are formed directly between CD1 and the sulfatide, whereas two additional hydrogen bonds are mediated by water molecules—one between the sulfate group and the backbone nitrogen of Gln154 and the other between the keto group of the fatty acid and the backbone oxygen of Met69. The same CD1 residues are involved in hydrogen bond formation with the short-chain alpha-GalCer ligand PBS-25 [PDB: 1Z5L]. Although several residues of the alpha1-helix (Asp80, Arg79, and Met69) provide specific contacts to the ceramide backbone, the alpha2-helix (Asp153, Thr156, and Gln154) is more involved in stabilizing the galactosyl headgroup. Nevertheless, Arg79 hydrogen bonds to the 6′ hydroxyl group of the galactose, thereby fixing the orientation of galactose between the alpha1- and alpha2-helices in concert with Asp153, which interacts with the 2′ hydroxyl group on the opposite side of the galactose.

column43: ""The peptide binding to HLA-Cw3 displays characteristics of the classical MHC class I peptide-binding mode in which both termini are securely anchored by a conserved pattern of hydrogen bonds and the middle residues form an arch above the floor of the cleft. Side chains from three of the nine residues, P4, P7 and P8, point out of the binding cleft. Of the other six residues, five of them, P1, P2, P3, P5 and P9, are at least 90% buried and P6 is 72% buried. The dimorphic positions Ser 77 and Asn 80 hydrogen bond with the P9 amide nitrogen and carboxylate, respectively. One feature notably missing in HLA-Cw3 as compared with HLA-Cw4 [PDB: 1IM9] and other class I molecules is a conserved hydrogen bond between Lys 146 and the P9 carboxylate. Instead, Lys 146 of HLA-Cw3 forms a salt bridge with KIR residue Asp 183. A tyrosine in place of serine at position 9 of HLA-Cw3 significantly restricts the size of the P2 pocket, rendering it more similar to HLA-A2 than to HLA-Cw4. As a result, the P2 pocket favors alanine in HLA-Cw3 and tyrosine in HLA-Cw4."" KIR binding imposes the peptide preference at position P8.

column43: The PC molecule is bound to mCD1d with the acyl chains inserted in the A' and F' pockets, and the hydrophilic phosphocholine extending from the central opening of the cleft toward the protein surface. The A' pocket of mCD1d is occupied by the longer acyl chain of PC linked to position 2 of glycerol that is typically esterified by unsaturated chains. The chain adopts a curved conformation pivoting around a pole formed by residues Cys12 and Phe70. The conformation of the chain suggests that fatty acids bearing up to four double bonds, such as arachidonic acid, could optimally fit the C-shaped A' pocket. No unsaturation was modeled in the bound Ag due to the intermediate resolution of the crystallographic data. The acyl chain is bound to the protein exclusively via van der Waals’ interactions. However, the side chains of Gln14, Ser28, Thr37, and His38 extend in the A' pocket within 4.5 Å of the acyl chain and are poised for hydrogen bonding with donors or acceptors branching from the hydrocarbon chain. The volume of the A' cavity of mCD1d can fit up to 28 methyl groups, and, similarly to other lipid-binding proteins, shorter acyl chains can be accommodated. The F' pocket is a linear, hydrophobic groove extending from the central opening of mCD1d toward the C-terminal end of the alpha1 helix. The residues lining this pocket are exclusively hydrophobic. The electron density for the hydrocarbon chain observed extending from the C1 atom of glycerol in the F' pocket is considerably shorter (C12) than that found in the A' pocket and adopts a fully extended conformation. Further extension of the acyl chain in the cavity by more than four methylene groups is prevented by a wall of hydrophobic residues formed by Phe81, Val85, Ile96, Ile98, and Phe120. Six CD1 residue, Y73, S76, R79, D80, G155, T156 make potential hydrogen bonds with the ligand; only one of them are among calculated contacts.

The majority of the peptide side chains overlay each other. However, the side chain of Tyr3 of HuD is rotated 110° compared with its analogue Phe3 in Tax, pointing the side chain toward the base of the peptide binding groove. Likewise, the side chain of Phe5 is rotated 120° compared with its analogue Tyr5 in Tax, also pointing the side chain toward the base of the binding groove. The concerted difference in the positions 3 and 5 side chains is attributable to differences in π-stacking between the two aromatic side chains: in HuD, Tyr3 and Phe5 are arranged in a classic parallel-displaced arrangement, whereas in Tax they are arranged in a T-shaped fashion.

column43: ""The mobility of the nonphosphorylated pHLA [PDB: 3FQN] is markedly reduced in the phosphorylated pHLA structure (this structure), and the entire epitope is clearly visible. Consistent with the other 2 phosphorylated complexes [PDB: 3FQU, 3FQX], the phosphate moiety is observed in 2 different conformers, which indicates a general theme of a mobile phosphate group. P2-Leu and P10-Ala represent the primary anchor residues, with P3-Asp and P6-Ile also projecting downward toward the antigen-binding cleft. The stabilization of the flexible nature of this peptide by phosphorylation can be attributed to stabilizing intrapeptide interactions as well as to interactions with Arg 65 and Lys 66 of HLA A2. In one conformer, the phosphate group interacts with P7-His and Arg 65 and it appears that the P7-His is “pulled in” toward the phospho-moiety compared with the nonphosphorylated complex. There is also a water-mediated H-bond between the phosphate group and P1-Tyr.""

column43: There are no conformational changes in the HLA A2 heavy chain associated with the accommodation of the phospho-moiety in this complex in comparison with the complex with non-phosphorylated peptide [PDB: 3FQT]. However, the peptide undergoes local conformational changes around the site of phosphorylation at P5 to avoid steric clashes with Ala 69 and Thr 73 of the HLA A2 heavy chain. ""This results in the peptide pushing away from the alpha1-helix toward center of the antigen-binding cleft, resulting in a shift of 2 Å in the Calpha position between P5 and P5-phosphoSer and also a change in the conformation of P3-Leu. Moreover, the phosphate group is observed in 2 discrete conformations, indicative of discrete mobility in this moiety [Table S1]. One conformer forms a salt bridge with P8-Arg, and both conformers interact with the peptide backbone through a water-mediated H-bond to P6-Pro, which appear to be the only interactions the phosphate head group makes. In this instance, these pHLA complexes define a case of altered self in which the peptide antigen demonstrates significantly altered conformation. These data demonstrate the alteration of a self-pHLA by a posttranslational modification.""

column43: The phosphopeptide adopts an extended conformation in the HLA-DR1 binding groove resembling that of non-phosphorylated peptides bound to MHC class II molecules. The primary anchor residues are Tyr5 (P1) and Ala10 (P6), in agreement with the requirement for an aromatic or large hydrophobic residue at P1 and a small uncharged residue at P6 for efficient binding to HLA-DR1. An unusual feature of the phospho-MART-1 peptide is that N-terminal residues P-3 (Pro2) and P-2 (Pro3), which lie outside the binding groove, are well ordered in the structure. In other peptide–MHC class II complexes, by contrast, these residues (when present) are generally not clearly defined in the electron density, indicating flexibility. Another notable feature of pMART-1 is that its main chain makes a nearly 90° turn at P-2 Pro3, causing P-4 Ala1 and P-3 Pro2 to point upward from the alpha1/beta1 platform of HLA-DR1. This orientation suggests the possibility of TCR contacts to the ordered N-terminus of the peptide.

The most noticeable difference between the GP2 complex and the other two is also the position of the P5 side chain. In the mutated epitope complexes residue P5, instead of pointing toward the alpha1 helix, points toward solvent and does not interact with any MHC residue in the peptide binding groove. Comparing HLA-A2/GP2(I2L/V5L) with HLA-A2/GP2(I2L/V5L/L9V), shows conformational differences at the C-terminal end of the peptide as a result of the mutation at P9.

column43: This structure was compare by the authors with the structure of HLA-A2 with a native decameric peptide, called ELA-0, [PDB: 2GT9]. The center of the ELA-0 peptide zig-zags throughout the HLA-A2 peptide binding groove. The center of ELA-1 (in this structure) also zig-zags, but does so in the opposite direction, bending towards and above the alpha1 helix at the AMBA spacer. Overall, the path adopted by ELA-1 through the HLA-A2 peptide binding groove diverges substantially from that of ELA-0, especially in the region replaced by the synthetic spacer. Thus, the distance between the nitrogen of the AMBA spacer of ELA-1 and that of Gly6 of ELA-0, intended to occupy similar positions, is 6.7 Å. The replacement of the native glutamate with a beta-alanine at the N-terminus had significant structural consequences. Compared to a standard amino acid, beta-alanine introduces an additional carbon-carbon bond between the first carbonyl oxygen and the peptidomimetic N-terminus; this additional bond forces the N-terminus out of the HLA-A2 P1 pocket, resulting in the loss of a hydrogen bond to Tyr171 of the HLA-A2 heavy chain that is conserved in all peptide/HLA-A2 structures in which the P1 pocket is occupied. The N-terminus instead points up out of the pocket, displacing the side chain of Lys66 by 3.2 Å due to charge and steric repulsions. This remarkable movement of Lys66 results in the loss of another conserved peptide-HLA-A2 hydrogen bond, from Lys66 to the carbonyl oxygen of the leucine at peptide position 2. The shift in Lys66 also removes a salt-bridge made with Glu63 that is conserved in the majority of peptide/HLA-A2 complexes.

column43: The peptide was bound in an extended conformation with a central bulge between P5 and P7. The central part of the peptide was relatively mobile as evident from the high B factors and the overall weak observable electron density for residues P5-P7. A striking feature within the bulge was the P5-Arg side-chain orientation, which extended almost parallel to the peptide and formed a salt bridge with Glu 19 of the MHC alpha1 helix. On both sides of the central bulge, the aromatic side chains of the partially buried residues at P3 (His) and P8 (Phe) contacted each other within the peptide binding groove and thereby bridged across and underneath the bulged residues via π-stacking interactions. This interaction appeared to establish a noncovalent end-to-end connection within the peptide and, together with the extended conformation of P5 (Arg), may be important for stabilizing the backbone conformation at the base of the bulge, thereby imposing constraints on the possible peptide conformations. The overall arrangement of the peptide rendered most residues partially or completely surface exposed so that only P2 (Pro) and P11 (Leu) were completely inaccessible. Contacts are provided in Supplemental Table III.

column43: Overall, this structure is similar to one with the wild-type peptide [PDB: 3ROO]. However, although the protrusion of p1K out of the peptide-binding cleft in H-2Kb/gp33 results [PDB: 2F74] in a significant modification of the position of the nitrogen atom of residue p2A when compared to p1A in H-2Kb/gp34 [PDB: 3ROO] or H-2Kb/NY-gp34 [PDB: 3ROL], this does not affect the conformation of the cluster of tyrosine residues that surround the N-terminal part of the peptide. ""Thus although the N- and C- peptide termini play crucial roles in binding of epitopes within the peptide-binding cleft formed by the alpha1alpha2 groove, these are not always necessarily required."" Nitrotyrosination of p3Y alters only the conformation of the H-2Kb heavy chain residue E152 which, in order to accommodate the side-chain of p3NY, undergoes a large conformational modification in H-2Kb/NY-gp34 when compared to H-2Kb/gp34. The rest of the H-2Kb peptide-binding groove is not affected by the nitrotyrosination of the peptide in H-2Kb/NY-gp34 when compared to H-2Kb/gp34. Two additional interactions are formed between peptide residue p3NY and the heavy chain residues Q114 and Y116 in the H-2Kb/NY-gp34 peptide when compared to H-2Kb/gp34, suggesting that nitrotyrosination of the peptide may result in higher stabilization capacity of H-2Kb complexes by NY-gp34 when compared to gp34.

column43: This HLA-A2-CLG structure explained effects of alpha2 helix mutation Q155A, which increased affinity by ∼10-fold, and alpha2 helix mutations Y159A and K146A, which eliminated binding. Q155 packs closely against L5 residue of the peptide, potentially interfering with TCR binding. Also, Q155 points directly up toward the TCR, whereas L5 protrudes toward the alpha2 helix, thereby presenting a less prominent target for the TCR. This suggests Q155 acts as a “gatekeeper” for NB20 allorecognition, as for self-restricted TCR/MHC binding, and its reorientation may be required during NB20/HLA-A2-CLG interaction to facilitate optimal allopeptide contacts.  Y159 presents a low profile to NB20, protruding laterally toward the groove. However, by interacting with CLG at P1–P3, it stabilizes its conformation around the flexible G3–G4 region. The drastic effect of Y159A may therefore reflect perturbation of CLG structure in the absence of these contacts. Similarly, K146 also points toward CLG, hydrogen-bonding with M8. K146 therefore stabilizes CLG conformation in an energetically critical region for TCR binding, and may also directly contact NB20; in such case, its CLG-specific conformation would be a component of antigen-specific recognition. Hence, the drastic effects of Q155A, Y159A, and K146A highlight similarities with self-restricted TCR/MHC interactions and the highly peptide-specific nature of NB20 allorecognition.

column43: The structure of the HLA-B*57:01–RVAQ–abacavir complex [PDB: 3VRI] was very similar to that of the HLA-B*57:01–LTTK–abacavir complex (this structure). Within both complexes, abacavir was bound in an extended manner, at the base of the antigen-binding cleft, in which the plane of the aromatic rings were positioned approximately diagonally across the cleft’s beta-sheet, with the cyclopentyl and purinyl moieties located in the D and E pockets, respectively, while the cyclopropyl moiety extended towards, and protruded into, the F pocket. Abacavir made extensive contacts with the HLA molecule, forming numerous van der Waals contacts, five hydrogen bonds and three water-mediated hydrogen bonds, yet made few contacts with the self peptides bound within the cleft, with direct abacavir–peptide contacts being limited to the P10-Ile in this RVAQ complex. ""The extensive contacts made by HLA-B*57:01 and the three moieties of abacavir provided a basis for understanding why only abacavir, and not its closely related metabolites (such as carbovir), was specifically bound within the antigen-binding cleft. Specifically, the cyclopentyl moiety of abacavir nestled against Tyr 99, in which the O1 moiety hydrogen-bonded to Tyr 74-OH, whereas the purinyl moiety of abacavir was flanked by aromatic residues Tyr 74 and Trp 147, as well as forming van der Waals contacts with Val 97, Ser 116 and Ile 124. Moreover, the N4 group of the purinyl moiety hydrogen-bonded to Asp 114, and the N1 and N2 groups hydrogen-bonded to Ser 116. The cyclopropyl moiety, which resided within the F pocket, packed against Ser 116 and Tyr 123 and additionally formed van der Waals contacts with Ile 95. The presence of the cyclopropyl group within the F pocket would disfavour the presence of larger amino-acid side chains at the PΩ position, thereby providing a basis for understanding why the presence of abacavir induces a preference for smaller residues at PΩ.

column43: When the structures of the mCD1d-Glc-DAG-s2 complex in the presence or absence of the TCR are compared, important conformational changes are observed for the ligand. In the absence of the TCR, the vaccenic acid encircles the A′ pole in a clockwise manner, the opposite orientation is preferred in the ternary complex, although residual density also suggests some equilibrium between the two orientations. Moreover, upon TCR ligation, the glucose moiety is shifted by about 30 degrees clockwise around its glycosidic bond to assume a position at the center of the binding groove as observed for other TCR-bound glycolipid antigens. Similar to what has been described for BbGL-2c, this conformational change requires the breaking of several contacts with CD1d and the formation of new hydrogen bonds with the alpha2 helix of CD1d and the TCR alpha chain. In particular, a hydrogen bond with Arg79 on the alpha1 helix is lost while new polar contacts are formed with Asp153 and Thr156 on the alpha2 helix upon TCR binding, resulting in a final orientation conserved among alpha-linked sugars. The presence of glucose on Glc-DAG-s2 results in an additional H bond between the antigen and the backbone of the alpha2 helix of CD1d, involving the carbonyl group of glycine 155A superposition of the mCD1d-Glc-DAG-s2 (this structure) and mCD1d-BbGL-2c complexes in presence of the TCR shows that the two hexose groups are oriented slightly differently at the opening of the binding groove, in the result, the novel hydrogen bond is formed between G155 on the alpha2 helix of CD1 and the 4′-OH of Glc-DAG-s2.

column43: ""Comparison of the main chain structure of HLA B3501 with the main chains all other MHC class I alleles that have been determined to date reveals an alteration in position of the N-terminal region of the alpha2 helix. The change in position of the alpha2 helix is from residues 141–152 and is some four to five times greater (1.5 Å) than the coordinate error."" ""The Nef peptide N terminus is positioned 1.5 Å higher in the B3501 A pocket than the standard N-terminal position. This is facilitated by a water molecule, which occupies a position equivalent to the N-terminal nitrogen of other peptides complexed with MHC class I alleles. This water molecule allows hydrogen bonds from conserved MHC side chains to peptide main chain atoms to be maintained. These hydrogen bonds hold the peptide N terminus in the A pocket and are observed in all MHC class I structures determined to date. As a result of the raised position of the peptide N terminus in the A pocket, the Pro anchor at P2 also sits higher in the B pocket."" ""The five polymorphic residues that are different between B53 and B3501 are clustered in the region of the F pocket and result in a change in specificity of this pocket for the PC. column43: This structure of alphaF54C overall was very similar to WT [PDB: 3QXA] except for a region proximal to the alphaF54C mutation, for which large differences were observed specifically in one of the two molecules in the asymmetric unit. The conformational changes involve a loop between two strands of the beta-sheet platform, the short 3-10 helix encompassing residues alphaL45 to alphaF50 at the edge of the binding site, and the extended stand region alphaF51 to alphaF54. The conformational change results in a ∼20° reorientation of the short 3-10 helix, together with a partial unwinding toward a more canonical alpha-helical pitch. These changes are accompanied by a concerted set of rotamer changes in residues that surround the P1 pocket. Large changes are observed for alphaF48, which positions its side chain on the side of the P1 pocket, displacing betaF89, which also undergoes a rotamer change, and for alphaL45, which moves to contact betaW153, replacing the contact normally made by the alphaF48 side chain. The rearrangements of alphaL45, alphaF48, and betaF89 resulted in changes in the shape and volume of the P1 pocket. The conformational changes in the 3-10 helix and adjacent strand region appear to be induced by contact at the alphaF51 position in molecule 2 of the asymmetric unit with another molecule in the crystal. The contact is observed for both WT and alphaF54C, but only in the mutant is the conformational change induced.

The outward-shifted alpha1 helix observed in the unliganded CD1d presenting LPC is shifted 2.3 Å inward, closing the A’ pocket and adopting a conformation close to that observed in the CD1d–alphaGalCer structures. In addition, the phosphorylcholine headgroup is shifted ~7.5 Å towards the A’ pocket, making room to accommodate the CDR loops of the TCR that occupy the position of the unliganded LPC headgroup, which is discussed in more detail later. This movement includes breaking of hydrogen bonds and a salt bridge between the negatively charged phosphate group and the positively charged Arg79 of CD1d in the unliganded state. In the liganded state, LPC is stabilized by hydrogen bonds with His68 of CD1d, which moves into hydrogen-bonding distance through the inward shift of the alpha1 helix and a salt bridge with K71 from iNKT TCR's HV4alpha loop. Overall, the contacts made between CD1d and the headgroup of LPC are almost completely unique between the liganded and unliganded states, with only a van der Waals (VDW) interaction with Trp153 shared between the two positions. Contacts with LPC are provided in Figure 5 and include CD1 residues C: H68, I69, V72, W153.

column43: The overall structure and peptide-binding mode were similar to those of HLA-B*51:01 complexed with the same Pol283-8 peptide [PDB: 1E28]. The replacement of Phe67 of HLA-B*51:01 with Ser in HLA-B*52:01 makes a local space, causing the N-terminal region of the peptide (T1 and A2) to reside deeper in the peptide-binding groove. Furthermore, the Gln63Glu mutation in HLA-B*52:01 affords a new interaction with the T1 residue of the peptide. These changes would, to some extent, have hidden the side chains of T1 and A2 (flat surface) from the TCRs, which may have reduced their interactions with TCRs on the HLA-B*52:01-restricted CTLs. On the other hand, the conformation of the C-terminal region of the peptide complexed with HLA-B*51:01 or HLA-B*52:01 was similar, even though C-terminal Ile8 of the peptide exhibited shallower penetration of the hydrophobic groove in the case of HLA-B*52:01 than in that of HLA-B*51:01. These results may indicate that the relatively flat surface of the N-terminal side of the peptide contributed to the lower affinity for TCRs in the case of HLA-B*52:01.

column43: The comparison of this structure of the NPM6I peptide with the wt-DbNP366  [PDB: 1HOC] showed that perturbations around the p6 position underpinned the observed functional impact of the mutant. In the WT-DbNP366, the P6M side-chain is exposed to the solvent and stabilized by stacking interactions with H155 of the H2Db molecule. The peptide mutation did not affect the overall structure of either H2Db or the peptide, but affected the flexibility of H155. The solvent-exposed conformation of H155 observed in the NPM6I structure is similar to that for the NPM6T escape peptide [PDB: 4HUW]. Interestingly, the P6I sat on the top of the H155 (second conformation observed), which became buried inside the Ag-binding cleft. This conformation of H155 was further stabilized by its interaction with P7E, the side-chain of which became partly buried relative to the wt complex [PDB: 1HOC]. The structural changes for H155 and P7E induced by P6I generated a more featureless pMHCI surface. Because residue 155 of MHC is important for TCR-mediated interactions, these alterations can potentially influence TCR binding.

column43: In complex with HLA-B*18:01, the SELEIKRY peptide adopted an extended conformation in which the peptide was characterized by minimal intramolecular contacts, consistent with an unconstrained conformation. The side chains of pE2, pI5, and pY8 pointed down toward the floor of the cleft, whereas pL3 was directed toward the alpha2-helix. The side chains of pS1, pE4, pK6, and pR7 pointed out of the cleft, with pE4, pK6, and pR7 highly solvent accessible and thus likely to play a role in directly contacting the TCR, consistent with the observed impact on T cell recognition of their substitution by an Ala. The SELEIKRY peptide was anchored to the cleft of HLA-B*18:01 primarily by pE2 and pY8. Namely, the side chain of pE2 formed hydrogen bonds to S24 and Y99, and a potential salt bridge to H9, as well as forming a network of water-mediated and van der Waals contacts with HLA-B*18:01. In addition to sharing extensive Van der Waals contacts with the MHC, the side chain of pY8 formed hydrogen bonds with R97 and S116. Contacts are provided in Table I.

column43: In complex with HLA-B*44:03, the EECDSELEIKRY peptide adopted a bulged conformation, with pR11 and the residues of the central bulged region (pD4–pI9) highly solvent exposed and therefore representing potential TCR contact points. This finding was consistent with the Ala substitution functional data, showing that pR11 and residues at the apex of the peptide bulge were critical for T cell recognition. Few interactions were observed between residues in the central region of EECDSELEIKRY and the HLA (Table I), which is consistent with the observed disorder in this region. Anchoring of EECDSELEIKRY to the cleft of HLA-B*44:03 was mediated predominantly by residues pE1, pE2, pK10, and pY12 (Table I), all of which were involved in multiple direct polar and ionic interactions with the MHC, in addition to forming a number of van der Waals and water-mediated contacts. Namely, the side chain of pE1 formed a salt bridge to R62 and R170 (not shown), whereas the side chain of pE2 interacted with Y9, K45, and Y99 and formed water-mediated interactions with T24, S67, and N70. The side chain of pK10 salt bridged with D114 and D116, whereas the side chain of pY12 hydrogen bonded to D116. Contacts are provided in Table I.

column43: There are conformational adjustments of the iGb3 head group after ligation of the NKT cell TCR. In the ligated state, the tri-hexosyl moiety extended toward the A′ pocket, lying flat against CD1d, such that iGb3 'hand clasped' the alpha2-helical axis, with the terminal sugar forming a 'finger grip' hold via a hydrogen bond to Thr159 and van der Waals interactions with Met162 of CD1d (Supplementary Table 4). The three sugar groups of iGb3 interacted with a span of the alpha2 helix (residues 153–162) characterized by small aliphatic residues, which enabled the iGb3 head group to closely abut CD1d. The terminal sugar moiety of iGb3 contacted only CD1d and not the NKT cell TCR. Similarly, the second glycosyl moiety formed many contacts with CD1d, including a hydrogen bond to Thr159, but formed limited contacts with the NKT cell TCR, in which the 6′-OH group formed hydrogen bonds to the framework residue Lys68alpha and to the carbonyl group of Asn30alpha. The proximal sugar group of iGb3 was 'bent over', akin to that in the ligated beta-GalCer conformation, forming interactions with Asn30alpha of the CDR1alpha loop and limited interactions with the CDR3alpha loop. Thus, to enable establishment of the consensus NKT cell TCR–CD1d–antigen docking topology, the iGb3 moiety was completely flattened after ligation of the NKT cell TCR.

column43: IPP bound in a shallow groove, with the surrounding residues conferring strong electrostatic interactions for the diphosphate moiety (Lys39, Arg61 and Gln102), as well as van der Waals interactions with the isopentenyl chain (Tyr100 and Tyr107). The hydrophobic residues Leu38 and Tyr100 lined the bottom of the binding pocket. Residues Lys39, Arg61 and Gln102 allowed indirect hydrogen-bond interactions mediated by three water molecules modeled in the binding site. The antigen-binding groove of BTN3A1 was much shallower than those of other APMs and had no deep antigen-binding pockets such as those of MHC, CD1 and MR1 molecules. Binding to BTN3A1 was highly dependent on electrostatic and hydrogen bonds, which fix the position of the phosphorylated antigen and pose heavy constraints on the structures that activate TCR Vgamma9Vdelta2 cells, as indicated by studies of the activation of cells by analogs of phosphorylated antigens. This mode of binding allows surface exposure of both charged and prenyl residues of bound antigens that might interact with the TCR. Comparison of the structures of BTN3A1–phosphorylated antigen complexes with that of 'empty' BTN3A1 [PDB: 4F8T, 4F8Q, 4F80] showed that a conformational change occurred after the phosphorylated antigen bound. Glu37 and Arg61, two amino acids that juxtaposed the antigen-binding pocket, moved their lateral chains away from the pocket, thus making more free space for IPP and HMBPP. Such structural changes might contribute to the slow association kinetics observed in the SPR experiments. In conclusion, the structural data showed that the distal domain of BTN3A1 bound both self and microbial phosphorylated antigens in a shallow pocket and formed a platform in which amino acid residues of both antigen and BTN3A1 might interact with the TCR.

column43: In the structure, the primary anchor residues for gp100(44–59) bound to HLA-DR4 are Leu48(P1) and Thr53 (P6); the secondary anchor residues are Glu51 (P4), Glu54 (P7), and Gln56(P9). By contrast, none of the secondary anchors (P4 Glu51, P7 Glu54, and P9 Gln56) conform to the optimal binding motif for HLA-DR4. Thus, the P4 pocket of HLA-DR4, which is lined by beta-chain residues Phe26, Lys71, Ala74, and Tyr78, is hydrophobic and prefers nonpolar residues. The charged C-group of the P4 Glu51 side chain points toward the surface of HLA-DR4 instead of into the P4 pocket. The P7 pocket of HLA-DR4, formed by beta-chain residues Try47, Trp61, Leu67, and Lys71, is likewise hydrophobic, such that the side chain of P7 Glu54 adopts a conformation very similar to that of P4 Glu51. The side chain of P9 Gln56 projects deep into the primarily nonpolar P9 pocket of HLA-DR4, which is formed by alpha-chain residues Asn69, Ile72, and Met73 and beta-chain residues Tyr37, Asp57, and Trp61. P9 Gln56 makes extensive van der Waals contacts with these residues, in addition to two side-chain–side-chain hydrogen bonds: P9 Glu56 Oε1–Oη DR4 Tyr37beta and P9 Glu56 Nε2–Odelta1 DR4 Asp57beta. The conformation of the bound peptide was directly compared with those of three other peptides that bind HLA-DR4: (1) a self-peptide from collagen II (CII1168–1180) binding HLA-DR4 with relatively high affinity; (2) a foreign peptide from influenza virus HA307–319  also binding HLA-DR4 with high affinity; and (3) a self-peptide from MBP111–129, binding weakly to HLA-DR4. The main chain of gp100(44–59) superposes very closely onto those of the peptides 1 and 2, from residues P2 to P9; and all three peptides sit deeply in the binding groove. By contrast, the peptide 3 diverges from all other peptides at anchor residues P6 and P7, due to a longer side chain at P6. The consequent elevation of MBP111–129 results in fewer contacts to HLA-DR4 compared with other peptides.

column43: Tyrosine at position 4 (p4Y) in gp33 [PDB: 1S7Q] projects down into the D pocket of H-2Kb formed by residues Q114, E152, L156, and Y159, where it is involved in the formation of three hydrogen bonds with the side chains of E152 and R155. The side chain of p4Y is further stabilized by hydrophobic interactions with the side chains of Y159 and p6F, whereas the main chain forms a hydrogen bond with N70. The structures of H-2Kb in complex with either the gp33 index peptide or the gp33 (Y4F) variant (this structure) are very similar. The hydroxyl group of p4Y forms a hydrogen bond with the NH1 atom of R155. The pY4F mutation breaks this hydrogen bond, allowing the R155 side chain to take a slightly different conformation, with the Nε atom moving 1.4 Å toward the C terminus of the peptide. The loss of the hydroxyl group also affects the side chain of residue E152, which forms a hydrogen bond with the tyrosine hydroxyl in the H-2Kb/gp33 index peptide structure, While, in general, the pY4F substitution does not result in any major structural changes at the MHC/peptide interface besides subtle movements of alpha2 TCR contact residues.

column43: ""In the H-2Db/gp33 complex [PDB: 1S7U], both residues p4Y and p6F project out of the peptide binding cleft, acting as potential main TCR contacts. The escape mutants pY4F [PDB: 1S7X] and pF6L [PDB: 1S7V] could thus be explained by impaired TCR recognition rather than by impaired MHC binding. However, the structural impacts of these two conservative substitutions are different. The pY4F mutation does not result in any modifications other than the removal of the tyrosine hydroxyl group, whereas the conserved pF6L substitution results in changes in the potential TCR contact residues that probably affect the sensitive regions of the TCR through direct sterical clashes and/or the introduction of cavities at the TCR/pMHC interface. The pF6L mutation results in shifts in the central portion variant peptide (residues p4 to p7). In contrast, the crystal structures of H-2Db/index gp33 and H-2Db/gp33 (Y4F) are remarkably similar. column43: The overall structures of Kb-VV-A11R [PDB: 3TIE] and Kb-LCMV-gp34 [PDB: 3TID] differ very little. Both peptides at P4 and P7 have solvent-exposed side chains that protrude away from the Kb H chain and are available for TCR contact. The combination of the bulky side chains at P6 and P7 with the P4N in a different conformation may help to explain the absence of a cross-reactive T cell response toward OVA.

column43: ""Clear electron density exists for a ligand in our MR1 structure, enclosed by the aromatic (Y7, Y62, W156), basic (R9, K43, R94), and polar (S24 and T34) residues lining the A′ cavity. The electron density is similar in nature to the 6-FP previously identified as bound by human MR1 refolded in the presence of mammalian cell-culture media [PDB: 4GUP]. Because MR1 used for this study was expressed in insect cells, there may be alternative compounds that can be presented that are either synthesized by insect cells or present in the insect cell media. The continuous electron density of this ligand with lysine 43 suggested that some, if not all, of this ligand was covalently attached via a Schiff base, as noted previously."" In the complex, bovine MR1 adopted an overall binary structure of a class I MHC fold associated with the beta2m subunit highly similar to that of HLA-A2 and to the human MR1 structure. MR1 has a cavity smaller (∼760 Å) than that of classical class I MHC molecules, similar to that noted previously.

column43: The structure of HPVG-D5 bound to HLA-B*35:01 adopted a different conformation compared with the HLA-B*35:08-HPVG-D5 [PDB: 4PRD] and caused rearrangements within the HLA-B*35:01 cleft itself. The HPVG-D5 conformation was constrained within the HLA-B*35:01 Ag binding cleft, whereby the central region of HPVG peptide (P5-P8) formed one helical turn and was stabilized by intrapeptide contacts. The helical turn enabled the P5-Asp to salt-bridge with Arg-97, the conformation of which was also impacted by the insertion of P9-Phe into the Ag binding cleft. Moreover, P8-Tyr also inserted its aromatic ring between the helical turn of the peptide and the HLA alpha2-helix. Accordingly, within HLA-B*35:01, structural rearrangements compensate for the shorter side chain of the P5-Asp to improve peptide-HLA interactions and internal peptide constraints.

column43: The HPVG-Q5 peptide did not markedly affect the overall antigen binding cleft conformation of either HLA-B*35:01 (this structure)(r.m.s.d. of 0.11 Å) or HLA-B*35:08 [PDB: 4PRE](r.m.s.d. of 0.22 Å). Namely, the P5-Gln flipped outward and became solvent-exposed and thus no longer contacted Arg-97 at the base of the Ag binding cleft. To compensate, P7-Asp reoriented from its surface-exposed position within the HLA-B*35:08-HPVG complex [PDB: 2F23] to act as a secondary anchor and salt bridge with Arg-97. Although the HPVG-Q5 structure was similar between the two HLA molecules (r.m.s.d. of 0.29 Å), conformational differences were observed around position 156. Namely, the Leu-156 of HLA-B*35:01 allowed the P7-Asp to sit 1 Å deeper in the binding cleft compared with the HLA-B*35:08 structure, in which the large Arg-156 occupied this region.

column43: The structures of the epitope-HLA-DP2 complex [PDB: 4P4R and 4P57] were compared to that bound to AV22 TCR in the presence of Be2+ (this structure). There are two unexpected features of this complex. First, the Be2+ moiety captured is the Be2+ cation itself, not a larger complex of Be2+ already partially ligated by solvent-derived electron donors (water, hydroxyl, carbonate, etc.). Second, both the Be2+ and Na+ are not accessible on the surface of the complex, so that the AV22 TCR must recognize some change in the complex surface induced indirectly by the Be2+ and Na+.

column43: In the HLA-DP5·Cry j 1(9-mer) structure, the nine residues of the accommodated Cry j 1 peptide (KVTVAFNQF) are clearly visible in the electron density map and occupy the p1-to-p9 binding pockets. Lys(p1), Phe(p6), and Phe(p9) are the “anchoring residues”, and their side chains are buried within their corresponding pockets formed along the peptide-binding groove of HLA-DP5. The HLA-DP5·Cry j 1 and HLA-DP2·pDRA complex [PDB: 3LQZ] structures superimposed on each other almost perfectly, with an rmsd value of 1.0 Å for the equivalent Calpha atoms. In the HLA-DP5 and HLA-DP2 structures, the P1, P4, P6, and P9 pockets are significantly deeper than the P2, P3, and P7 pockets. However, each of the four deeper pockets of HLA-DP5 has a different position, size, or charge from that of the corresponding pocket of HLA-DP2. The bottom of the P1 pocket of HLA-DP5 consists of Gln31alpha and Asp84beta and is negatively charged. Therefore, the HLA-DP5 P1 pocket is suitable for accommodating a positively charged amino acid residue, such as Lys. In contrast, the bottom of the HLA-DP2 P1 pocket is hydrophobic. The acidic P1 pocket is also present in some class II HLA structures, such as HLA-DQ2, HLA-DQ2.3, and HLA-DQ8. On the other hand, the P4 pocket of HLA-DP5 has a positive charge (Lys69beta), whereas that of HLA-DP2 has three negative charges (Glu26beta, Glu68beta, and Glu69beta). The distance between the P6 and P9 pockets of HLA-DP5 is shorter than that of HLA-DP2; the Tyr28beta side chain shifts toward the P9 pocket and hydrogen bonds with Asn(p7)(Cry j 1). Furthermore, the diameter and the depth of the P9 pocket are larger in HLA-DP5 than in HLA-DP2 due to the differences between Glu55beta(HLA-DP5) and Asp55beta(HLA-DP2) and between Leu35beta(HLA-DP5) and Phe35beta(HLA-DP2).

column43: The overall structural features of the this complex and  H-2Db/MimA2 [PDB: 3WS6] were very similar. Structural alignment of the two peptides demonstrated a root-mean-square deviation of 0.207 Å for the nine equivalent Calpha atoms, suggesting that the overall conformation of the two peptides was almost the same. The orientations of the side chains of each residue of the two peptides were also comparable. In both cases, N at P5 is buried in a polar pocket formed by E9, Q70, Q97, and Y156 of the H chain. The side chain of N at P5 forms hydrogen bonds with Q70 and Q97. L at P9 is deeply buried in a hydrophobic pocket defined by the H chain residues F116, I124, T143, and W147. In addition to these two conserved anchor residues, calculation of available and buried surface areas of each residue of MimA2 and YQLENYCGL revealed that the residue at P3 is also important for MHC binding. The hydrophobic residue at P3 (L in YQLENYCGL and I in MimA2) is deeply buried at the interface, which helps to stabilize the complexes. Importantly, and unique to YQLENYCGL, the Q at P2 is deeply buried in a polar pocket defined by the H chain residues E9, Y22, S24, and Y45 and forms hydrogen bonds with E9 and Y22. In contrast, the nonpolar A at P2 of MimA2 cannot make such contacts and is not involved in anchoring the peptide to the MHC H chain. The presence of the auxiliary anchor at P2 of YQLENY and YQLENYC helps to explain how these peptides, despite lacking a C-terminal anchor residue, can form stable complexes with H-2Db and spontaneously elicit AI4-like T cell responses in nearly all NOD mice.

column43: In this structure, CD1c adopts an architecture highly similar to CD1c-MPM [root mean square (RMS) deviation = 0.319 Å] [PDB: 3OV6] with an MHC-like fold with the two hydrophobic pockets called A′ and F′ shared by all human CD1 molecules. The A′ pocket accommodated the alkyl chain of PM, whereas the F′ pocket exhibited an open groove-like structure, similar to that in the CD1c/MPM structure. Omit and 2Fo-Fc maps show clear electron density for the PM alkyl tail and phosphate head group bound in CD1c. The methylated lipid chain of PM traverses through the A′ pocket, bent in a clockwise manner around the A′ pole to fit within the tunnel, exiting through the D′ portal. Overall, the PM alkyl tail superimposed with that of MPM with a RMS deviation of 1.6 Å, confirming that methylated mycoketide tails mediate CD1c binding and thereby serve as a molecular pattern for mycobacterial detection. In contrast to the similarities in alkyl chain positioning, the phosphate head group of PM, lacking the mannose moiety found in MPM, is positioned ∼6 Å from its equivalent position in the CD1c/MPM structure, adopting a more extended conformation toward the F′ pocket. The phosphate head group of PM is stabilized by several possible H-bonds with main chain atoms of Tyr73 and Leu77 of the alpha1 helix of CD1c.

column43: This peptide and ALQDA peptide [PDB: 4U6X] bind with the canonical P2-Leu into the B pocket and with non-canonical PΩ-Val residues in the F-pocket for HLA-A*02:01, a methionine for the FNLKD peptide, and an isoleucine for the ALQDA peptide. The FNLKD peptide was well defined in the cleft of the HLA-A*02:01 molecule, and is the longest well defined epitope observed in complex with a HLA class I molecule to date. The FNLKD bulges out of the HLA-A*02:01 cleft forming a beta-sheet hairpin structure from P7 to P12 residues. The secondary structure formation in the bulged part of the peptide made intra-molecular contacts, constraining and rigidifying the peptide, and probably explains how the FNLKD can be such a long peptide and being so rigid in HLA-A*02:01 cleft. The stable conformation of the FLNKD was also associated with a higher number of contacts with the HLA-A*02:01 molecule, with the peptide engaging 11 of its residues to interact with the HLA, and making a total of 215 contacts (6 salt bridges and 14 hydrogen bonds).

column43: The structures of Mamu-B*17 complexed with eight different immunogenic SIV-derived peptides were determined. Superposition of all eight peptides revealed the structural basis for length heterogeneity within Mamu-B*17–restricted epitopes. The majority of bound peptides adopt similar conformations with the P2 and C-terminal (Pc) residues serving as anchors, consistent with other pMHC I structures. Exceptions to this rule are HW8 and GW10. For HW8, His1 occupies pocket B to serve as the N-terminal anchor residue. For GW10, the two small amino acids Gly1 and Ser2 at the N terminus occupy pocket A, which results in P3 serving as an anchor residue. In accordance with previous studies, the primary anchor specificity at the C terminus was found to be associated with aromatic residues (W and F), which is similar to the situation for HLA-B*57–restricted peptides. Conversely, the N-terminal anchor residues for Mamu-B*17 appear to have a broad chemical specificity (R, H, T, Q) due to the adjustment of pocket B (discussed below). In addition, the secondary anchor residues (Pc-2 or Pc-3) also display diverse conformations.
